## 1. Program Overview

- **Full official program name:** HOME Investment Partnerships Program
- **Administering federal agency:** U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)[1][3][5].
- **Local government role:** Local governments, known as *participating jurisdictions* (PJs), receive formula grants from HUD to design and administer affordable housing programs tailored to their community’s needs. They are responsible for planning, implementing, and monitoring HOME-funded activities, often in partnership with local nonprofits and community organizations[1][3][4].

## 2. Eligible Activities

Local governments can use HOME funds for a variety of affordable housing and community development activities, including:
- **Acquisition, construction, or rehabilitation of affordable rental housing**[1][2][3].
- **Assistance to homebuyers for purchase and/or rehabilitation of homes**[1][2][3].
- **Tenant-based rental assistance (TBRA) for low-income households**[1][2][3].
- **Rehabilitation of owner-occupied housing to improve safety, accessibility, and energy efficiency**[1][3].
- **Development of transitional and permanent housing for individuals and families experiencing or at risk of homelessness**[4].
- **Support for Community Housing Development Organizations (CHDOs) to develop affordable housing**[3][5].
- **Accessibility modifications for persons with disabilities**[1][3].

## 3. Citizen Participation Requirements

Federal regulations (24 CFR Part 91) require robust citizen participation in the planning and implementation of HOME-funded activities:
- **Public hearings and comment periods:** Local governments must hold at least one public hearing and provide a public comment period (typically 30 days) during the development of the Consolidated Plan and Annual Action Plan[1][3].
- **Community needs assessment:** The planning process must include an assessment of local housing and community development needs, with opportunities for residents to provide input[1][3].
- **Resident advisory committees or councils:** While not mandatory, many jurisdictions establish advisory committees or councils to ensure ongoing resident input, especially from low-income and minority populations[1].
- **Annual planning and reporting:** The Annual Action Plan and Consolidated Annual Performance and Evaluation Report (CAPER) both require public review and comment before submission to HUD[1][3].

## 4. Leverage Points for Residents

Residents can influence local HOME funding decisions through several mechanisms:
- **Participation in public hearings and comment periods** during the development of the Consolidated Plan, Annual Action Plan, and CAPER[1][3].
- **Engagement in community needs assessments** by attending meetings, responding to surveys, or submitting written comments[1][3].
- **Serving on advisory committees or councils** if established by the local government[1].
- **Contacting local government staff** responsible for the HOME program, typically found in the housing, community development, or planning departments (e.g., Community Development Director, Housing Program Manager, or Consolidated Plan Coordinator)[1][3].

## 5. Reporting & Compliance

- **Annual reporting requirements:** Participating jurisdictions must submit a Consolidated Annual Performance and Evaluation Report (CAPER) to HUD, detailing how HOME funds were used and progress toward meeting goals[1][3].
- **Performance metrics tracked:** Metrics include the number and type of housing units produced or rehabilitated, households assisted, affordability periods maintained, and progress toward addressing identified community needs[1][3].
- **Public availability of reports:** The Consolidated Plan, Annual Action Plan, and CAPER must be made available for public review, typically via the local government’s website and at public libraries or government offices[1][3].

## 6. Key Resources

- **Official federal program URL:**  
  [https://www.hudexchange.info/programs/home/](https://www.hudexchange.info/programs/home/)[5]
- **Citizen participation plan requirements URL:**  
  [https://www.hudexchange.info/programs/consolidated-plan/citizen-participation/](https://www.hudexchange.info/programs/consolidated-plan/citizen-participation/) (see 24 CFR Part 91)[3]
- **Annual allocation/formula information URL:**  
  [https://www.hudexchange.info/programs/home/home-allocations/](https://www.hudexchange.info/programs/home/home-allocations/)[5]

**Federal regulation:** 24 CFR Part 91 governs citizen participation and planning requirements for the HOME program[3].

## Program Overview

**Full official program name:**  
Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Program (HCVP)[1][3][4].

**Administering federal agency:**  
U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)[1][2].

**Description (local government role):**  
The Section 8 HCVP is a federally funded rental assistance program that helps low-income families, seniors, and individuals with disabilities afford safe, decent housing in the private market[1][2]. HUD provides funding and oversight, but local implementation is managed by Public Housing Agencies (PHAs), which determine eligibility, issue vouchers, inspect units, and pay subsidies directly to landlords on behalf of tenants[1][2]. PHAs also maintain waiting lists, conduct outreach, and ensure compliance with federal regulations.

## Eligible Activities

Local governments (through PHAs) can use Section 8 HCVP funds to support a range of housing and community development activities, including:

- **Issuing tenant-based vouchers** that allow eligible households to choose and lease privately owned housing (apartments, single-family homes, townhouses) that meets program standards[1][2][3].
- **Administering project-based vouchers** tied to specific housing developments, increasing the stock of affordable units in targeted neighborhoods[1][3].
- **Providing mobility counseling** to help voucher holders access neighborhoods with greater opportunities (schools, jobs, services)[1].
- **Supporting homelessness prevention** by prioritizing vouchers for individuals and families experiencing or at risk of homelessness (as allowed by local preferences)[1].
- **Ensuring housing accessibility** by working with landlords to modify units for people with disabilities and prioritizing accessible units in project-based developments[3].
- **Conducting outreach and education** to landlords and tenants about program rules, rights, and responsibilities[2].
- **Collaborating with local service providers** to connect voucher holders with supportive services (e.g., job training, childcare, health care)[1].

## Citizen Participation Requirements

**Public hearings or comment periods:**  
PHAs must provide opportunities for public comment during the development of the Annual Plan and any significant amendments, as required by 24 CFR Part 903[1]. This typically includes public hearings and a comment period of at least 45 days.

**Community needs assessment:**  
PHAs must assess local housing needs and market conditions as part of their planning process, often through surveys, public forums, and analysis of demographic data[1].

**Resident advisory committees or councils:**  
PHAs are required to establish Resident Advisory Boards (RABs) composed of residents of public housing and participants in the HCV program to advise on policy development and program operations (24 CFR Part 903)[1].

**Annual planning and reporting with public input:**  
PHAs must prepare and publish an Annual Plan, which includes goals, objectives, and strategies for the coming year, and must solicit and consider public input during its development[1].

## Leverage Points for Residents

**Influencing local funding decisions:**  
Residents can attend public hearings, submit written comments, and participate in RABs to voice priorities for voucher allocation, landlord outreach, and supportive services[1].

**Participating in planning processes:**  
Residents should monitor PHA websites and local notices for announcements about Annual Plan development, public hearings, and comment periods. Engaging early in the process maximizes impact.

**Who to contact:**  
Residents should contact their local PHA’s executive director, resident services coordinator, or public information officer. For broader HUD-related questions, the local HUD field office can provide guidance[2].

## Reporting & Compliance

**Annual reporting requirements:**  
PHAs must submit an Annual Plan to HUD, which includes performance data, financial information, and a summary of public comments received[1].

**Performance metrics tracked:**  
Key metrics include the number of vouchers issued, lease-up rates, unit inspection pass rates, tenant rent burdens, and progress toward deconcentration and mobility goals[1].

**Public availability of reports:**  
Annual Plans, performance reports, and other key documents must be made publicly available, typically on the PHA’s website and at their offices[1].

## Key Resources

**Official federal program URL:**  
HUD’s Housing Choice Voucher Program page (search “HUD HCV program” for the current .gov URL)[2].

**Citizen participation plan requirements:**  
24 CFR Part 903 outlines resident participation requirements for PHAs[1].

**Annual allocation/formula information:**  
HUD’s Office of Public and Indian Housing provides annual funding notices and allocation formulas (search “HUD PIH funding notices” for the current .gov URL)[1].

---

This structured overview reflects federal regulations (especially 24 CFR Parts 903 and 982) and standard PHA practices, emphasizing both local government responsibilities and concrete opportunities for resident engagement.

## 1. Program Overview

- **Full official program name:** Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) Program
- **Administering federal agency:** Internal Revenue Service (IRS) under the U.S. Department of the Treasury[3].
- **Description (local government role):** The LIHTC program provides federal tax credits to state housing agencies, which then allocate these credits to private developers for the construction or rehabilitation of affordable rental housing[1][2][3]. Local governments often participate by supporting projects through zoning, infrastructure, gap financing, or by collaborating with state agencies to identify community needs and priorities for affordable housing development[2][3].

## 2. Eligible Activities

Local governments can support or facilitate the following activities through the LIHTC program:

- **New construction of affordable rental housing** for low- and moderate-income households[1][2].
- **Rehabilitation of existing rental housing** to preserve or improve affordable units[1][2].
- **Acquisition and preservation of at-risk affordable housing** to prevent loss of existing affordable stock[1][2].
- **Supportive housing development** for populations experiencing homelessness or with special needs (when paired with other funding sources)[3].
- **Accessibility improvements** to ensure compliance with ADA and fair housing requirements[3].
- **Site improvements and infrastructure upgrades** necessary for affordable housing development (often with local or state funds in conjunction with LIHTC)[2].
- **Mixed-income or mixed-use developments** that include a required percentage of affordable units[2].

## 3. Citizen Participation Requirements

While the LIHTC program itself is governed by federal tax law (26 U.S.C.A. § 42), **citizen participation is primarily required at the state and local level** through the Qualified Allocation Plan (QAP) process:

- **Public hearings and comment periods:** State housing agencies must hold public hearings and provide opportunities for public comment on their QAP, which sets priorities and selection criteria for LIHTC awards[3].
- **Community needs assessment:** The QAP process typically involves an assessment of local and statewide affordable housing needs, often informed by public input[3].
- **Resident advisory committees/councils:** Some states or localities may establish advisory groups to provide input on housing priorities, though this is not federally mandated for LIHTC[3].
- **Annual planning/reporting with public input:** Updates to the QAP and related planning documents generally require public notice and comment periods, allowing residents to influence priorities for LIHTC allocations[3].

## 4. Leverage Points for Residents

Residents can influence local LIHTC funding decisions in several ways:

- **Participate in public hearings or comment periods** during the QAP development or amendment process at the state housing agency[3].
- **Submit written comments or attend meetings** when local governments or housing authorities discuss affordable housing priorities or support for specific LIHTC projects[3].
- **Engage with local housing advisory boards, planning commissions, or city councils** that review or endorse LIHTC applications[3].
- **Contact roles such as the local housing director, planning department staff, or community development office** to learn about upcoming opportunities for input or to advocate for specific housing needs[3].

## 5. Reporting & Compliance

- **Annual reporting requirements:** Property owners must annually certify compliance with income and rent restrictions to the state housing agency, which reports to the IRS[2][3].
- **Performance metrics tracked:** Metrics include the number of affordable units created or preserved, tenant income levels, rent levels, and compliance with long-term affordability requirements (typically 15-30 years)[1][2][3].
- **Public availability of reports:** State agencies often publish annual reports or summaries of LIHTC allocations and project performance; these are generally available on state housing agency websites[3].

## 6. Key Resources

- **Official federal program URL:** [https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/low-income-housing-credit](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/low-income-housing-credit) (IRS official page)[3].
- **Citizen participation plan requirements URL:** While LIHTC is not governed by HUD’s 24 CFR Part 91 (which applies to CDBG/HOME), public participation is required in the QAP process. See your state housing agency’s QAP page for specific requirements; a directory is available at [https://www.novoco.com/resource-centers/affordable-housing-tax-credits/lihtc-allocating-agencies](https://www.novoco.com/resource-centers/affordable-housing-tax-credits/lihtc-allocating-agencies)[3].
- **Annual allocation/formula information URL:** [https://www.novoco.com/resource-centers/affordable-housing-tax-credits/lihtc-allocating-agencies](https://www.novoco.com/resource-centers/affordable-housing-tax-credits/lihtc-allocating-agencies) (state-by-state allocation info)[2][3].

**Key federal regulations:**  
- 26 U.S.C.A. § 42 (Internal Revenue Code, Section 42)[3].
- 26 C.F.R. § 1.42 (Treasury regulations)[3].

**Note:** Unlike HUD block grant programs, LIHTC does not have a single federal citizen participation regulation like 24 CFR Part 91, but state QAP processes must include public input opportunities[3].
